packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS node_identity (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY);   -- ULID
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: TEXT is SQLite's flexible-typing column; ULID is stored as a 26-char string. SQLite has no native fixed-length/varchar enforcement.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Use `text` or `char(26)`/`varchar(26)` with `primary key`. Postgres `text` works directly. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is also valid in modern Postgres.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: ver INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` is a rowid alias in SQLite: it auto-assigns a monotonically increasing integer on INSERT without AUTOINCREMENT, and crucially it is the rowid used by the FTS5 `content_rowid='ver'` link. Postgres has no rowid concept.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Use `ver bigint generated always as identity primary key` (or `bigserial`). The FTS5 content_rowid coupling disappears since Postgres FTS uses a tsvector column on the same row, so `ver` becomes a plain surrogate key.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: emb          F32_BLOB(${dim}),
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: F32_BLOB(dim) is a libSQL-only native vector column type (float32 blob with a fixed dimension). Not valid in standard SQLite or Postgres.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Install pgvector and use `emb vector(${dim})`. The dim substitution stays the same; the column type string changes from `F32_BLOB(<dim>)` to `vector(<dim>)`.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: valid_to INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 8640000000000000
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Relies on SQLite's 64-bit INTEGER to store the FOREVER sentinel (max JS Date ms = 8.64e15) and on epoch-ms integers for the temporal model. The literal sentinel is embedded in views, indexes, triggers and constraints.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Use `bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 8640000000000000` — Postgres bigint (max ~9.2e18) holds it fine. The sentinel-based half-open interval model ports unchanged; just bigint everywhere `valid_from`/`valid_to` appear.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS nv_emb_idx ON node_versions(libsql_vector_idx(emb, 'metric=cosine')) WHERE valid_to = 8640000000000000;
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `libsql_vector_idx(...)` is libSQL's function-expression ANN index builder with a metric option string; SQLite/Postgres have no such function. It is also a partial index (WHERE valid_to = FOREVER).
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: pgvector partial index: `CREATE INDEX nv_emb_idx ON node_versions USING hnsw (emb vector_cosine_ops) WHERE valid_to = 8640000000000000;` (or ivfflat). Metric is encoded by the ops class (`vector_cosine_ops`) instead of the `metric=cosine` string. Partial-index WHERE is supported by Postgres.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS nodes_fts USING fts5(body, content='node_versions', content_rowid='ver'); ... CREATE TRIGGER nodes_fts_ai AFTER INSERT ON node_versions BEGIN INSERT INTO nodes_fts(rowid, body) VALUES (new.ver, new.body); END;
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: FTS5 external-content virtual table plus a manual AFTER INSERT sync trigger keyed on the rowid (`ver`). FTS5 is SQLite-only; external-content + content_rowid wiring and the rowid-based trigger have no Postgres analog.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Add a `body_tsv tsvector` column (or generated column `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body,''))) STORED`) plus a GIN index `CREATE INDEX ON node_versions USING gin(body_tsv)`. No separate virtual table or sync trigger needed — the tsvector lives on the same row, so the `nodes_fts`/`nv ver IN (SELECT rowid ...)` join collapses to a direct `body_tsv @@ query` predicate. Note: a STORED generated tsvector covers historical versions too (closes are UPDATEs that don't touch body), matching the as-of-lexical intent.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS nodes AS SELECT ... FROM node_versions WHERE valid_to = 8640000000000000;
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Plain views (SQLite-compatible syntax). Not strictly SQLite-specific except the sentinel literal.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW nodes AS ...` ports directly (Postgres has no CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS; use CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW). Logic unchanged.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: await client.execute('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL'); await applyConnPragmas(client); await client.executeMultiple(schema(dim));
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL is SQLite-only. `executeMultiple` is a libSQL client method that runs a multi-statement script without splitting on `;`.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Drop the PRAGMA entirely (Postgres has WAL by default, no per-DB setting needed). For multi-statement DDL, the `pg` driver can send a multi-statement string in a single simple-query, or run statements individually; there is no `executeMultiple` so the init path needs reworking to either a single multi-statement query or a loop.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: const info = await client.execute(`PRAGMA table_xinfo(${table})`); if (!info.rows.some((r) => String(r.name) === col)) { await client.execute(ddl); }
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `PRAGMA table_xinfo(<table>)` is SQLite's column-introspection pragma (xinfo variant shows hidden/generated columns). SQLite has no `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, forcing this check-then-ALTER guard. Table name is string-interpolated into the PRAGMA.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres supports `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, eliminating the guard entirely. If introspection is still wanted, query `information_schema.columns`. The generated-column visibility issue (table_info hiding generated cols) doesn't exist in Postgres.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: weight REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 1.0 CHECK (weight >= 0)
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: REAL is SQLite's floating storage class; CHECK constraint syntax is standard. Mostly portable.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Use `real` or `double precision` (Postgres `real` exists). CHECK clause ports verbatim.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: node_analytics (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY ...) -- UPSERTed by P8 jobs
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Comment references UPSERT (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT) done by P8 analytics jobs; the table itself is standard. Listed because the area's DDL anticipates ON CONFLICT upserts (a SQLite/libSQL ON CONFLICT clause, also valid in Postgres).
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ...` is supported identically in Postgres. The actual upsert SQL is in P8 (not these files); the DDL ports cleanly.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: emb          F32_BLOB(${dim}),
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: F32_BLOB(dim) is a libSQL-only column type for fixed-dim float32 vectors stored as a BLOB; standard SQLite has no vector type.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Use pgvector: `emb vector(768)`. Requires `CREATE EXTENSION vector`. Stored as a first-class typed column; no per-dim BLOB encoding needed.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE INDEX ... ON node_versions(libsql_vector_idx(emb, 'metric=cosine')) WHERE valid_to = 8640000000000000;
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: libsql_vector_idx() is libSQL's expression-based ANN index builder (DiskANN-style); the 'metric=cosine' config and the function wrapper are libSQL-specific. It's a PARTIAL index over live rows only.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: pgvector partial HNSW or IVFFlat: `CREATE INDEX nv_emb_idx ON node_versions USING hnsw (emb vector_cosine_ops) WHERE valid_to = 8640000000000000;` Cosine metric is chosen via the opclass (vector_cosine_ops) rather than a string config. Postgres supports partial indexes natively, so the WHERE clause ports directly.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS nodes_fts USING fts5(body, content='node_versions', content_rowid='ver');
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: FTS5 virtual tables with external content (content=/content_rowid=) are an SQLite-only full-text mechanism; they store no copy of the text and reference the base table by rowid (ver).
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres uses a tsvector column + GIN index instead of a separate virtual table. Either add `body_tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body,''))) STORED` with `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN(body_tsv)`, or index an expression directly. No external-content virtual table; the FTS lives on the same table.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: CREATE TRIGGER nodes_fts_ai AFTER INSERT ON node_versions BEGIN INSERT INTO nodes_fts(rowid, body) VALUES (new.ver, new.body); END;
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: External-content FTS5 does not auto-sync, so an AFTER INSERT trigger manually mirrors rows. This trigger (and the DROP-during-bulk-load + 'rebuild' command) is entirely an artifact of FTS5 external-content tables.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: With a STORED generated tsvector column, NO trigger is needed — the column maintains itself and the GIN index updates automatically. If using a plain tsvector column instead, a BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE trigger calling tsvector_update_trigger() handles it. The 'rebuild' / DROP-index-during-bulk-load optimization maps to dropping/recreating the GIN index around COPY.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: ver          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is a SQLite rowid alias — auto-assigned monotonic integer used both as `ver` and as the rowid joined by vector_top_k (n.rowid=v.id) and FTS content_rowid='ver'. The rowid==PK identity is SQLite-specific.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Use `ver bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY` (or bigserial). Postgres has no rowid; since vector_top_k/FTS rowid joins go away in the pgvector/tsvector rewrite, `ver` simply becomes a normal surrogate key. The keyset pagination in temporal.ts (ORDER BY valid_from, ver) keeps working since ver stays a unique monotonic integer.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: valid_to INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 8640000000000000 (FOREVER = 8640000000000000)
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Stores epoch-ms timestamps as INTEGER with a sentinel FOREVER = max JS Date ms. SQLite's flexible typing stores this fine; the magic number is duplicated as a literal inside DDL and SQL strings.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Port as `bigint` columns (epoch ms) keeping the FOREVER sentinel literal unchanged — simplest and preserves the half-open [valid_from,valid_to) and partial-index predicates verbatim. (A timestamptz redesign is possible but would change the public time model and the FOREVER constant, so avoid for API stability.)

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: PRAGMA table_xinfo(${table}) ... uses table_xinfo not table_info because table_info HIDES generated columns
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: PRAGMA table_xinfo / table_info are SQLite introspection pragmas; the comment notes a libSQL-build-specific quirk about generated columns being hidden.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Query information_schema.columns / pg_attribute: `SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name=$1 AND column_name=$2`. Generated columns appear there (is_generated). Or use `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` which Postgres supports natively, removing the check-first guard entirely.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: await client.executeMultiple(schema(dim))
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: executeMultiple is a @libsql/client method that runs a multi-statement script without ;-splitting; the DDL is one big string.
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: node-postgres `pool.query(bigDdlString)` accepts multiple semicolon-separated statements in a simple (non-parameterized) query, so a single query call works. Or split and run sequentially. No executeMultiple equivalent name.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL; applyConnPragmas (foreign_keys, busy_timeout)
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: WAL journal mode, foreign_keys, busy_timeout are SQLite pragmas with no Postgres analog (Postgres is always MVCC/WAL and enforces FKs by default).
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Drop entirely. Postgres has WAL inherently, enforces foreign keys always, and connection-level timeouts map to statement_timeout/lock_timeout (set via SET or connection params). No per-connection pragma step needed.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: node_analytics ... UPSERTed by P8 jobs (per comment D4/B10)
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Comment references UPSERT (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT) used by analytics writers; SQLite and Postgres both support ON CONFLICT but exact syntax/EXCLUDED handling differs slightly. (Actual UPSERT SQL is outside these four files.)
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ... = EXCLUDED... is nearly identical to SQLite. Mostly portable; verify the conflict-target and partial-index-arbiter cases.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet:
export async function init(client: Client, dim?: number): Promise<void>
export function ensureColumn(client: Client, ...)
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `init` and `ensureColumn` are public and take a libSQL Client; ensureColumn uses `table_xinfo` (SQLite pragma-table function). NODES_FTS_TRIGGER_DDL and NV_EMB_IDX_DDL are exported SQLite-specific DDL strings (FTS5 trigger, libSQL vector index).
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: Retype `client` to DbClient. Replace `table_xinfo` introspection with information_schema.columns for Postgres (driver-specific introspection method). The exported DDL constants (NODES_FTS_TRIGGER_DDL, NV_EMB_IDX_DDL) are SQLite-only — for Postgres these become tsvector/GIN and pgvector index DDL; if they must stay exported, gate them behind the dialect or deprecate as libSQL-only constants.

packages/core/src/schema.ts.snippet: ver INTEGER PRIMARY KEY  (implicit rowid; FTS content_rowid='ver')
packages/core/src/schema.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` aliases SQLite rowid (monotonic auto-assigned), and FTS5 content_rowid='ver' depends on it. The rowid semantics drive vector_top_k row mapping (retrieve.ts comment about LIVE rowids).
packages/core/src/schema.ts.postgresApproach: ver BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (or BIGSERIAL). No rowid concept — the FTS rowid coupling and vector_top_k rowid-return mapping must be re-derived from the explicit PK/ANN ordering.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: await client.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON'); await client.execute('PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000');
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON` (SQLite needs FKs explicitly enabled per connection) and `PRAGMA busy_timeout` (SQLite lock-wait) are both SQLite-only and per-connection.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Both are unnecessary in Postgres: FK enforcement is always on, and lock waiting is governed by `lock_timeout`/`statement_timeout` (optionally set via SET, not a PRAGMA). The whole `applyConnPragmas` per-connection requirement goes away. Note: this is in db.ts (not one of the 4 listed files) but init() in schema.ts calls it.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: await client.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON'); await client.execute('PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000');
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: PRAGMA is SQLite/libSQL-only; foreign_keys defaults OFF in SQLite and does not persist per-connection, and busy_timeout is SQLite's lock-wait knob for its single-writer model. Both must re-run on every fresh connection.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Drop entirely. Postgres enforces FKs unconditionally (no per-conn toggle) and has no busy_timeout (MVCC, no global write lock); the analogous knobs are lock_timeout/statement_timeout set via SET or connection params, applied once per pooled session if at all.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: const base = cfg.syncUrl ?? process.env.SQLD_URL; const syncUrl = base ? `${base}/${namespace}` : undefined; const client = createClient({ url: `file:${namespace}.db`, authToken: ..., ...(syncUrl ? { syncUrl, syncInterval: cfg.syncInterval ?? 60 } : {}) });
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: This is the core libSQL embedded-replica model: a local SQLite file (file:<ns>.db) backed by a remote sqld primary at SQLD_URL/<namespace>, with background syncInterval pull. createClient, syncUrl, authToken, file: URLs and per-namespace sqld databases are libSQL-specific; there is no Postgres equivalent of an on-disk file replica per tenant.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Pick a tenant model. Closest analog to DB-per-tenant: connect to a distinct Postgres database (or distinct connection string) per namespace via a pooled pg/postgres.js client cache keyed by namespace — no local file, no embedded replica. More common in PG: schema-per-tenant (single DB, SET search_path TO <namespace> per checkout) or row-level (shared tables + tenant_id column + RLS policies). syncUrl/syncInterval/embedded-replica have no PG equivalent; read scaling is done with PG physical/logical read replicas at the connection level, not per-tenant files. authToken becomes normal PG role credentials held only by the server.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: const clients = new Map<string, Client>(); ... createClient({ url: `file:${namespace}.db`, ... });
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Per-namespace Client caching assumes a cheap embedded SQLite connection (one Client ~ one file). A Postgres client is a TCP connection/pool, so a 1:1 namespace->client map can exhaust connections.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Cache a pg Pool (or a search_path-setting wrapper) per namespace, or a single shared pool that issues SET search_path per checkout for schema-per-tenant. Bound total connections; consider a pgbouncer/RDS-proxy in front. Same Map keyed by namespace, different lifecycle (pools close, don't .close() per request).

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: export async function syncIfReplica(namespace){ if (process.env.SQLD_URL) await getDb(namespace).sync(); }
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: .sync() is the libSQL embedded-replica pull — it has no SQL/Postgres analog; it forces the local file to catch up to the sqld primary before serving (sync-before-serve, gates /ready).
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Remove. With PG read replicas there is no client-driven sync; readiness instead checks connectivity (SELECT 1) and optionally replication lag via pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()/pg_stat_replication. The Readiness latch in serve.ts stays but markReady() is gated on a connectivity/migration check instead of replica sync.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: c.close(); ... for (const c of clients.values()) c.close();
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Client.close() on a libSQL embedded client is a synchronous-ish cheap teardown of a file handle. Fine for SQLite.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Use pool.end() (async, returns a Promise) for each cached pool; closeAll/evict must await. Don't close a shared pool per request.

packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: DbConfig is the user-passed connection config object and it is 100% libSQL/sqld embedded-replica shaped: authToken (sqld JWT), syncUrl (sqld replication endpoint), syncInterval (replica pull cadence). None of these concepts exist in Postgres — there is no embedded-replica sync, and auth is a connection string user/password or a libpq DSN.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Generalize DbConfig into a driver-neutral shape: { connectionString?: string; ssl?: boolean | TlsOptions; poolMax?: number; statementTimeoutMs?: number }. Keep authToken/syncUrl/syncInterval ONLY in a libSQL-specific sub-config (e.g. a discriminated `driver: 'libsql' | 'postgres'` union, or a separate LibsqlConfig). For API compat, keep the three fields optional+deprecated on the base type so existing libSQL callers compile, and have the Postgres driver ignore them.

packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Returns a libSQL `Client`, hardcodes a `file:${namespace}.db` URL (one SQLite file per tenant) and reads SQLD_URL/SQLD_TOKEN env. The whole connection-per-namespace caching strategy assumes a file-or-sqld DB. Postgres cannot do one-physical-DB-per-namespace cheaply; namespaces become schemas or row-level tenant keys within a shared pool.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Introduce an abstract `DbClient`/driver interface (execute, batch, transaction, sync(no-op), close) that both `@libsql/client` and a node-postgres/postgres.js adapter implement. `getDb(namespace)` returns that interface, not the concrete libSQL Client. For Postgres, map namespace → schema (search_path) or a tenant-id column over a pooled connection rather than a per-namespace physical DB/file. `syncIfReplica` becomes a no-op for Postgres.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet:
await client.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON');
await client.execute('PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000');
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: applyConnPragmas is exported and runs SQLite PRAGMAs that have no Postgres equivalent (FK enforcement is always on in PG; busy_timeout maps loosely to lock_timeout/statement_timeout).
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Move per-connection setup behind the driver interface. Postgres adapter sets e.g. `SET statement_timeout`/`SET lock_timeout` instead of PRAGMAs. Keep `applyConnPragmas(client)` as a thin shim that delegates to the driver, or deprecate it from the public API in favor of driver-managed connection init.

packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `.sync()` is a libSQL embedded-replica method; the env gate SQLD_URL is sqld-specific. Postgres has no client-side replica sync — replication is server-side.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Keep the function name in the public API for source compat but make it a no-op when the driver is Postgres (the `sync()` capability becomes an optional method on the driver interface). The `/ready` readiness latch in serve.ts that pairs with this stays unchanged.

packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: One physical SQLite file per tenant namespace (file:<ns>.db), cached one Client per namespace. This file-per-tenant model is the core isolation guarantee and is meaningless in Postgres.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: Map each namespace to a Postgres schema (schema-per-tenant, SET search_path) or a separate database/role on one server, replacing file:<ns>.db with a connection pool keyed by namespace. authToken/syncUrl/syncInterval (embedded-replica) have no PG analog — drop or replace with pool config.

packages/core/src/db.ts.snippet: applyConnPragmas: PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON; PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000; syncIfReplica()->getDb(ns).sync(); evict/closeAll -> c.close()
packages/core/src/db.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Per-connection PRAGMAs and the embedded-replica .sync() are libSQL/SQLite-only. evict/closeAll close a single cached file Client; in PG you manage a pool, not a file handle.
packages/core/src/db.ts.postgresApproach: FK enforcement is always-on in PG (drop PRAGMA foreign_keys); busy_timeout -> statement_timeout/lock_timeout via pool config or SET. .sync() becomes a no-op. evict/closeAll -> pool.end() per namespace pool.

packages/core/src/constraints.ts.snippet: ALTER TABLE node_versions ADD COLUMN ${col} TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (json_extract(props, '$.${prop}')) VIRTUAL
packages/core/src/constraints.ts.whySqliteSpecific: SQLite VIRTUAL generated column using `json_extract(props,'$.prop')`. `VIRTUAL` (not stored) and `json_extract` with `$.path` JSONPath are SQLite-specific; the column is computed on read and indexable.
packages/core/src/constraints.ts.postgresApproach: Two options: (a) drop the generated column and index the expression directly — `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON node_versions ((props->>'prop')) WHERE ...`; or (b) Postgres generated columns must be `STORED` (no VIRTUAL), so `ADD COLUMN gp_x text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (props->>'x') STORED`. Expression index (a) is the closer match and avoids storage. Requires `props` to be `jsonb`.

packages/core/src/constraints.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `json_extract` with `$.x` path and `props` stored as TEXT is SQLite's JSON1 idiom. Returns SQL NULL when absent (NULLs distinct in the unique index).
packages/core/src/constraints.ts.postgresApproach: Store `props` as `jsonb` and use `props->>'x'` (text extraction) or `props->'x'`. `->>'x'` returns NULL when the key is absent, preserving the NULL-distinct uniqueness semantics.

packages/core/src/constraints.ts.snippet: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ux_${kind.length}_${kind}_${prop} ON node_versions(${col}) WHERE valid_to = ${FOREVER} AND kind = ${sqlLiteral(kind)}
packages/core/src/constraints.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Partial UNIQUE index filtered to live rows + kind. Partial indexes themselves are portable, but the FOREVER literal and the value being indexed (the SQLite generated col) tie it here. Identifier inlining + sqlLiteral are needed because SQLite can't bind identifiers in DDL.
packages/core/src/constraints.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres supports partial unique indexes verbatim: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ... ON node_versions((props->>'prop')) WHERE valid_to = 8640000000000000 AND kind = 'X'`. The safeIdent/sqlLiteral inlining stays (Postgres also can't parameterize identifiers/DDL). Index logic is identical.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `vector(?)` is libSQL's function that parses a JSON array string into an F32_BLOB. The B5 distinction (vector('[]') throws on dim 0, so omitted emb binds literal NULL) is a libSQL-vector quirk.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: With pgvector, bind the embedding as a vector literal/text and cast: `$8::vector` (the pgvector text format `[1,2,3]` is accepted directly), so `vector(?)` becomes `$n::vector`. NULL handling is simpler — pgvector accepts NULL without the dim-0 throw, so the two-branch B5 logic can collapse to one statement binding NULL or the vector.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: All parameterized SQL uses `?` positional placeholders (libSQL/SQLite style). Pervasive across every query in graph.ts.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres uses `$1, $2, ...` numbered placeholders. Every `?` must be rewritten to `$n` in order (or use a driver/query-builder that translates). Mechanical but touches essentially every SQL string in graph.ts; the relClause/idSub dynamic placeholder generation (`rels.map(() => '?')`) needs an index-aware generator.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `client.batch(stmts, 'write')` is a libSQL client API: an implicit atomic transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE..COMMIT) over an array of statements in one round trip. The `'write'` mode hint is libSQL-specific.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Wrap the statements in an explicit `BEGIN; ...; COMMIT;` on a `pg` client/pool connection (or use the driver's transaction helper). No `'write'` mode concept. The atomicity guarantee is the same; the API shape differs and must be re-implemented (likely a small `withTransaction` helper).

packages/core/src/graph.ts.snippet: tx = await this.raw.transaction('write'); // BEGIN IMMEDIATE (may throw SQLITE_BUSY)
packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `client.transaction('write')` opens a libSQL interactive transaction as BEGIN IMMEDIATE (write lock acquired upfront). The conditional-close + retry envelope is built around SQLite's single-writer lock model and busy_timeout=0 on interactive tx connections.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Use a pooled connection with `BEGIN; ... COMMIT/ROLLBACK`. Postgres uses MVCC + row-level locking, not a single global write lock, so the BEGIN IMMEDIATE semantics differ: serialize with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the live row or use `SERIALIZABLE`/`REPEATABLE READ` isolation. The conditional-close (`WHERE valid_to = FOREVER` + check rowsAffected) ports as an optimistic-concurrency pattern. tx.closed/rollback API maps to pg client methods.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Retry classification keys off SQLite error codes (SQLITE_BUSY/LOCKED) and 'database is locked' messages — SQLite's lock-contention failure mode under concurrent writers.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres equivalents are serialization failures: SQLSTATE `40001` (serialization_failure) and `40P01` (deadlock_detected), plus `55P03` (lock_not_available) when using `NOWAIT`. The retry loop + backoff structure stays; only the error-code matcher changes. Under MVCC many of these contention cases vanish, but SERIALIZABLE retries on 40001 are still needed.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.snippet: WHERE src = ? AND rel = ? AND valid_to = ? [args: ..., FOREVER]
packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: The FOREVER sentinel (8640000000000000) drives every live-row predicate; it's bound as an integer arg. Portable in principle but coupled to the bigint sentinel model.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Identical predicates against `bigint` columns; bind FOREVER as a bigint/number. No change beyond column type and placeholder syntax.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.snippet: where.push('nv.ver IN (SELECT rowid FROM nodes_fts WHERE nodes_fts MATCH ?)'); args.push(match);
packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: FTS5 `MATCH` operator against the external-content virtual table, joined back via `rowid = ver`. The match expression is FTS5 query syntax (quoted tokens OR-joined, ftsMatch at lines 460-466).
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: With a `body_tsv tsvector` column, replace the subquery with a direct predicate `nv.body_tsv @@ to_tsquery('english', $n)` (or `websearch_to_tsquery`). The ftsMatch token-quoting/OR-joining is reworked to tsquery syntax (`tok1 | tok2`). No rowid subquery needed.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.snippet: applyLimit(`... ORDER BY n.id`, maxRows) / LIMIT ${Math.floor(maxRows)}
packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: LIMIT clause and string-interpolated maxRows; SQLite LIMIT syntax. Portable.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: LIMIT ports verbatim to Postgres. No change beyond placeholder style if LIMIT were parameterized (here it's interpolated).

packages/core/src/graph.ts.snippet: JSON.stringify(storedProps) stored into props TEXT; JSON.parse(String(cur.props)) on read
packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `props` is a TEXT column holding JSON serialized in JS and re-parsed in JS (SQLite stores JSON as text). No server-side JSON typing.
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Store `props` as `jsonb`. The `pg` driver returns jsonb as a parsed JS object automatically (so JSON.parse on read may be dropped) and accepts JS objects for binding (JSON.stringify may be dropped depending on driver config). This also enables the `props->>'x'` constraint path. Behavioral parity needs care so callers still receive the same parsed shape.

packages/core/src/graph.ts.snippet:
import type { Client, InStatement, InValue, Row, Transaction } from '@libsql/client';
constructor(public raw: Client, public schema: S, upcasters?: UpcasterRegistry)
packages/core/src/graph.ts.whySqliteSpecific: The most load-bearing leak: `Graph` (the primary data-layer class) exposes `public raw: Client` — a libSQL Client — and P4/P6/P7 read `graph.raw` directly (retrieve, history, journey all take `graph.raw`). Constructor positional arg #1 is a libSQL Client. Also imports libSQL value types (InStatement/InValue/Row/Transaction).
packages/core/src/graph.ts.postgresApproach: Change `raw`'s type to the abstract driver interface (DbClient) that both libSQL and Postgres adapters satisfy, and replace InStatement/InValue/Row/Transaction with driver-neutral aliases (e.g. SqlStatement, SqlValue, ResultRow, DbTransaction). Because `retrieve`, `history`, `journey` consume `graph.raw`, the driver interface must cover everything they call. The constructor signature stays positionally identical (Client→DbClient is source-compatible for libSQL callers since the libSQL Client structurally satisfies the interface).

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.snippet: FROM vector_top_k('nv_emb_idx', vector(?), ?) v JOIN node_versions n ON n.rowid = v.id
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: vector_top_k() is a libSQL table-valued function that takes the index NAME as a string literal and returns rowids ranked by ANN distance; vector(?) parses a JSON/text array into an F32_BLOB. There is no equivalent table-function-by-index-name pattern in Postgres, and it returns SQLite rowids (joined back via n.rowid) which Postgres lacks.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: Express ANN directly as an ORDER BY on the distance operator with a LIMIT, letting the planner pick the HNSW index: `SELECT id FROM node_versions WHERE valid_to=FOREVER ORDER BY emb <=> $1::vector LIMIT $2` (<=> = cosine distance). No index-name string, no rowid join. The query embedding is bound as a `::vector` cast of a text array instead of vector(?). Note: pgvector applies the index based on the column+opclass, so the partial-index live filter must be in the WHERE to match the partial index.

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.snippet: SELECT n.id AS id, MIN(v.id) AS rk ... GROUP BY n.id ... ORDER BY rk LIMIT ? (k * 4 over-fetch)
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: The MIN(v.id) trick uses the libSQL vector_top_k rowid as an ANN-rank proxy (lower rowid != lower distance in general, but here v.id is the index's returned order). The whole over-fetch-then-temporal-filter dance exists because the libSQL ANN index is PARTIAL over live rows and cannot see historical versions at :t.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: In pgvector you'd order by actual distance, so capture the real score: `ORDER BY MIN(emb <=> $1)`. The over-fetch + EXISTS temporal filter logic itself is portable (plain SQL), but you can rank by true cosine distance instead of a rowid proxy, improving correctness.

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.snippet: walk AS ( SELECT ... 0 AS depth, ',' || n.id || ',' AS path ... UNION ALL ... walk.path || n.id || ',' ... WHERE walk.depth < ? AND walk.path NOT LIKE '%,' || n.id || ',%')
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Recursive CTE is standard SQL and ports, BUT the cycle guard uses a string-concatenated path with LIKE '%,'||id||',%' — relying on SQLite's `||` concat and LIKE. The id-list is delimited-string encoded. This works in Postgres but `||` with NULL and LIKE semantics differ subtly; also Postgres recursive CTEs forbid aggregates/DISTINCT in the recursive term and have stricter UNION typing.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: Recursive CTE ports nearly verbatim. Prefer Postgres arrays for the cycle guard: `path text[]` with `WHERE NOT (n.id = ANY(walk.path))` and `walk.path || n.id`, which is cleaner and avoids delimiter-injection edge cases. `||` string concat works in PG too but array form is idiomatic. Watch UNION ALL column type unification (depth int, body/uri text).

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.snippet: SELECT id, body, uri, MIN(depth) AS depth FROM walk GROUP BY id ORDER BY depth
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Bare columns (body, uri) selected alongside MIN(depth) with GROUP BY id only — SQLite's relaxed GROUP BY / bare-column 'any value' behavior. Postgres rejects non-grouped, non-aggregated columns.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres requires every selected column to be grouped or aggregated. Use `DISTINCT ON (id) id, body, uri, depth ... ORDER BY id, depth`, or wrap with a window: `MIN(depth) OVER (PARTITION BY id)` then filter, or add body/uri to GROUP BY (safe since they're functionally dependent per id-at-min-depth). DISTINCT ON is the clean idiom.

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.lines: all SQL; hybrid all SQL; temporal all SQL
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.snippet: args: [qEmbJson, k] with `?` placeholders; rel IN (${rels.map(()=>'?').join(',')})
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Positional `?` placeholders bound by textual order — the code comments emphasize 'Param order = textual SQL order' and manually push args per CTE side. libSQL/SQLite uses `?`.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres uses numbered `$1,$2,...` placeholders. Either switch the driver to one that translates `?`→`$n` (e.g. @libsql/client's pg-compatible layer or a shim), or rewrite all arg-building to numbered params. The duplicated as-of binds (t pushed 2x/4x) get error-prone with $n; consider named params. This is pervasive across all three SQL files.

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Dynamic `?` placeholder generation for IN-lists, with the same fragment emitted per adjacency side (forward+reverse), requiring args pushed twice. Tightly coupled to positional binding.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres idiom is `rel = ANY($n::text[])` binding the rels array ONCE regardless of count or number of CTE sides — eliminates the per-side arg duplication and the dynamic placeholder string entirely. Significant simplification opportunity.

packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.snippet:
import type { Client } from '@libsql/client';
export function retrieve(raw: Client, embed: EmbedFn, opts): ...
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `retrieve` (the GraphRAG entrypoint) takes a libSQL Client positional arg #1 and runs libSQL vector search (vector_top_k / vector distance) inside.
packages/core/src/retrieve.ts.postgresApproach: Retype `raw` to DbClient. The vector search inside must be re-expressed against pgvector (`<=>`/`<->` operators, ivfflat/hnsw index) by the Postgres adapter; the public signature `retrieve(raw, embed, opts)` is unchanged.

packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.snippet: SELECT id, vector_extract(emb) AS e FROM node_versions ... ; JSON.parse(String(row.e))
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.whySqliteSpecific: vector_extract() is the libSQL function that turns an F32_BLOB back into a JSON text array for client-side parsing. Postgres pgvector returns the vector type directly.
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.postgresApproach: `SELECT id, emb FROM node_versions ...` — pgvector serializes vector to its text form `[a,b,c]` over the wire; parse client-side (or use a driver that maps it). No extract function needed; you can also keep MMR cosine entirely in SQL if desired.

packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.snippet: FROM nodes_fts JOIN node_versions n ON n.ver = nodes_fts.rowid WHERE nodes_fts MATCH ? AND n.valid_to = FOREVER ORDER BY rank LIMIT ?
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `nodes_fts MATCH ?` is FTS5 match syntax; `ORDER BY rank` uses FTS5's built-in bm25 ranking pseudo-column; the join via nodes_fts.rowid = n.ver is the external-content linkage.
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.postgresApproach: `SELECT id FROM node_versions WHERE body_tsv @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english',$1) AND valid_to=FOREVER ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(body_tsv, websearch_to_tsquery('english',$1)) DESC LIMIT $2`. No join to a separate table; @@ is the match operator; ts_rank_cd replaces the rank column. websearch_to_tsquery also subsumes much of sanitizeMatch's job.

packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.snippet: sanitizeMatch: split whitespace, wrap each token "..." (doubling "), join with ' OR '
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Builds an FTS5 MATCH query-string grammar (quoted phrases joined by OR). The escaping rules (doubling embedded double-quotes, FTS5 operators AND/OR/NOT/NEAR/*/^/:) are FTS5-specific.
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.postgresApproach: Replace with `websearch_to_tsquery('english', userInput)` which safely parses free user text (handles quotes/operators) with NO manual sanitization, or `plainto_tsquery` for pure AND/OR-free matching. The public export sanitizeMatch may need to stay for API stability but its body becomes Postgres tsquery building or a no-op passthrough.

packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.snippet: WITH seeds(id) AS (SELECT value FROM json_each(?))
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.whySqliteSpecific: json_each() is SQLite's JSON1 table-valued function used to explode a JSON array of seed ids bound as a single text param into rows.
packages/core/src/hybrid.ts.postgresApproach: Use `unnest($1::text[])` with a bound array (the libSQL pg driver supports text[] params), or `SELECT value FROM json_array_elements_text($1::json)`. unnest is the idiomatic, fastest choice and avoids JSON entirely.

packages/core/src/temporal.ts.snippet: keyset: WHERE (valid_from > ? OR (valid_from = ? AND ver > ?)) ORDER BY valid_from, ver LIMIT ?+1
packages/core/src/temporal.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Plain ANSI SQL keyset pagination — portable. Only SQLite-specific aspect is `?` placeholders and the INTEGER-PK `ver` tiebreak. The row-value comparison could be tightened in PG.
packages/core/src/temporal.ts.postgresApproach: Ports directly; optionally use the row-value comparison `(valid_from, ver) > ($1,$2)` which Postgres supports natively and is cleaner than the OR-expansion. Placeholders become $n.

packages/core/src/pattern.ts.whySqliteSpecific: json_extract() with a SQLite JSON path string ('$.key') is the SQLite JSON1 API; props stored as TEXT JSON.
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.postgresApproach: Store props as jsonb; filter with props->>'key' = $n (text) or props @> jsonb_build_object('key', $n). The '$.key' path syntax does not exist in Postgres; jsonb_path_query / #>> are the analogs.

packages/core/src/pattern.ts.snippet: WITH RECURSIVE adj(a,b) AS (...), walk(id,anchor,depth,path) AS (... walk.path || adj.b || ',' ... WHERE walk.depth < ${v.max} AND walk.path NOT LIKE '%,' || adj.b || ',%')
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Cycle-safety uses a comma-delimited TEXT path accumulated via `||` and tested with NOT LIKE; depth bound interpolated as a literal. Works in SQLite but the string-concat/LIKE cycle guard is an idiom, and `||` concatenation of an integer id relies on SQLite's loose typing.
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres supports WITH RECURSIVE. Use an array path: path int[]/text[], path || adj.b, and NOT (adj.b = ANY(path)) — far cleaner and avoids substring false-positives. Or use the SQL-standard CYCLE clause. Integer-to-text concat needs explicit casts.

packages/core/src/pattern.ts.whySqliteSpecific: SQLite auto-coerces ids/ints in `||` concatenation; relies on dynamic typing.
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres requires text operands for ||; cast (id::text) or use a text[]/array path. ULID ids are TEXT so concat is fine, but any integer operand must be cast.

packages/core/src/pattern.ts.whySqliteSpecific: min/max/maxDepth are interpolated as numeric literals into SQL rather than bound. Not dialect-specific but matters when porting placeholder strategy ($n).
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.postgresApproach: Same interpolation works; or bind as $n. Already int-validated in code paths, low risk.

packages/core/src/pattern.ts.snippet: raw.execute({ sql: capped, args: args as never[] }); ... `WHERE (${keyCols.join(', ')}) > (${key.map(() => '?').join(', ')})`
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Positional `?` placeholders (libSQL). Row-value tuple comparison `(a,b) > (?,?)` for keyset pagination is supported by both, but placeholder style differs.
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.postgresApproach: Rewrite `?` to `$1..$n` (node-postgres). Row-value comparison (a,b) > ($1,$2) is supported in Postgres identically. Wrap-and-GROUP-BY/ORDER-BY pagination pattern carries over.

packages/core/src/pattern.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Half-open temporal predicate against FOREVER-sentinel valid_to (8640000000000000 stored as INTEGER). Not dialect-specific syntactically but tied to the FOREVER sentinel design (see db.ts).
packages/core/src/pattern.ts.postgresApproach: Same predicate works with bigint columns; keep FOREVER as a bigint sentinel, or switch to NULL valid_to + COALESCE. If kept, bind FOREVER as $n / literal bigint.

packages/core/src/journey.ts.snippet: WITH RECURSIVE deg(...) AS (...), journey(node,t_arrive,depth,path) AS (SELECT ?, CAST(? AS INTEGER), 0, ',' || ? || ',' UNION ALL SELECT ${nextExpr}, MAX(j.t_arrive, e.valid_from), ... j.path || ${nextExpr} || ',' ... WHERE j.depth < ? AND j.path NOT LIKE '%,' || ${nextExpr} || ',%' AND (deg.c IS NULL OR deg.c <= ${maxFanout}))
packages/core/src/journey.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Same TEXT-path cycle guard idiom; `MAX(a,b)` is SQLite's scalar 2-arg MAX (in Postgres MAX is an aggregate — this is the single biggest gotcha here); CAST(... AS INTEGER) for the from-timestamp.
packages/core/src/journey.ts.postgresApproach: WITH RECURSIVE works. Replace scalar MAX(a,b) with GREATEST(a,b) (critical — MAX would error/aggregate). Use array path + ANY() cycle guard. CAST AS INTEGER -> ::bigint. maxFanout interpolation fine or bind $n.

packages/core/src/journey.ts.snippet: j.path || ${nextExpr} || ',' ... 'CASE WHEN e.src = j.node THEN e.dst ELSE e.src END'
packages/core/src/journey.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Concatenating node ids (TEXT ULIDs) with `||`; the `both` direction builds next-node via CASE. Concat of TEXT is fine; the cycle-guard LIKE substring approach can false-positive on id prefixes (mitigated by comma delimiters).
packages/core/src/journey.ts.postgresApproach: Switch to array path with = ANY to avoid substring issues; CASE expression is identical in Postgres.

packages/core/src/journey.ts.snippet: WHERE e.valid_to = ${FOREVER} ... JOIN edge_versions e ON ${edgeMatch} AND e.valid_to > j.t_arrive
packages/core/src/journey.ts.whySqliteSpecific: FOREVER (8640000000000000) interpolated as a literal to mean 'live row'; depends on the sentinel-valued valid_to design (D3).
packages/core/src/journey.ts.postgresApproach: Same predicate with bigint, FOREVER as literal/param; or NULL valid_to with valid_to IS NULL. Keep consistent across the codebase.

packages/core/src/journey.ts.whySqliteSpecific: `->>` JSON extraction on a TEXT JSON column (SQLite supports ->/->> since 3.38). Result is TEXT.
packages/core/src/journey.ts.postgresApproach: props->>'name' works identically on jsonb (returns text). With jsonb no JSON.parse needed for whole-doc reads (driver returns objects); here props_json is re-parsed in JS so behavior is preserved.

packages/core/src/journey.ts.snippet: await withTimeout(raw.execute({ sql: applyLimit(sql, limits.maxRows), args: params }), limits.timeoutMs, o.metrics)
packages/core/src/journey.ts.whySqliteSpecific: raw.execute({sql,args}) is the libSQL client call shape; applyLimit injects a SQLite LIMIT.
packages/core/src/journey.ts.postgresApproach: raw.query(text, values) shape in node-postgres; $n placeholders. LIMIT injection identical. Behind a client interface this is a thin adapter change.

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.snippet: `SELECT src, dst, weight FROM edges WHERE 1 = 1${relIn} ORDER BY src, dst` with rel IN (${rels.map(()=>'?').join(',')})
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Positional `?`, dynamic IN-list expansion, reads from `nodes`/`edges` now-views.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: $n placeholders; prefer `rel = ANY($1::text[])` over expanded IN-lists in Postgres. Views port directly.

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Half-open snapshot predicate tied to FOREVER sentinel; snapshotCSR routes t>=FOREVER to the live path to avoid a false `t < valid_to`.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: Identical predicate on bigint; keep the FOREVER routing or switch to NULL valid_to semantics.

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.snippet: WITH RECURSIVE walk(node,cost,path,depth) AS (SELECT ?,0.0,',' || ? || ',',0 UNION ALL SELECT e.dst, w.cost + ${costExpr}, w.path || e.dst || ',', w.depth+1 ... WHERE w.node <> ? ${depthClause} AND w.path NOT LIKE '%,' || e.dst || ',%' ORDER BY w.cost + ${costExpr}) SELECT cost,path FROM walk WHERE node = ? ORDER BY cost LIMIT 1
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: ORDER BY *inside* the recursive CTE to make it a best-first/priority-queue walk is a SQLite-specific behavior — SQLite processes the recursive queue honoring the CTE-level ORDER BY (a documented SQLite extension). Standard SQL / Postgres does NOT allow ORDER BY in the recursive term and would reject or ignore it, breaking the priority-queue semantics. Plus TEXT-path cycle guard.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres forbids ORDER BY in a recursive CTE term. Reimplement: either (a) enumerate paths in the CTE without ordering and ORDER BY cost LIMIT 1 in the outer query (correctness holds but no early pruning — can blow up), (b) use a Postgres recursive CTE with a CYCLE clause and outer ordering, or (c) prefer the in-memory Dijkstra path (mode:'memory') which is dialect-agnostic. This is the hardest single item to port faithfully.

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: String path built by `||` over ids; relies on implicit text coercion and LIKE-substring cycle detection.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: Use text[]/array path with NOT (e.dst = ANY(path)); cast non-text operands.

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.snippet: INSERT INTO node_analytics (id, ${metric}, computed_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?) ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET ${metric} = excluded.${metric}, computed_at = excluded.computed_at ... raw.batch(stmts.slice(...), 'write')
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: SQLite UPSERT syntax `ON CONFLICT(col) DO UPDATE SET x = excluded.x`; `raw.batch(stmts,'write')` is a libSQL client API for atomic multi-statement batches.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres supports nearly identical syntax: ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col (EXCLUDED uppercase; works lowercase too). `raw.batch()` has no pg equivalent — use a transaction (BEGIN/COMMIT) or unnest()-based bulk upsert. Column name `${metric}` is interpolated (whitelisted via Metric type).

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: libSQL `Client.batch(statements, mode)` — atomic batched execution with a write mode hint.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: node-postgres has no batch(); wrap statements in a client transaction (await c.query('BEGIN') ... 'COMMIT'), or pipeline. Need an abstraction over the client.

packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.snippet: const METRIC_COL: Record<Metric,string> = {...}; ... ORDER BY na.${col} DESC ... LIMIT ?
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Interpolated ORDER BY column guarded by a whitelist + Object.hasOwn (anti-injection). Not dialect-specific; LIMIT ? with positional placeholder.
packages/core/src/algorithms.ts.postgresApproach: Same whitelist approach; $n for limit. LIMIT supported identically.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.snippet: DROP INDEX IF EXISTS nv_emb_idx ... NV_EMB_IDX_DDL = CREATE INDEX ... ON node_versions(libsql_vector_idx(emb, 'metric=cosine')) WHERE valid_to = FOREVER
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: libsql_vector_idx() and the partial vector index are libSQL-native vector features; no SQLite/standard equivalent.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: Use pgvector: column type vector(dim); CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (emb vector_cosine_ops) (partial index WHERE valid_to = FOREVER is supported). Drop/recreate-around-bulk pattern still applies. This is a design-level swap of the vector subsystem.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: libSQL `vector(?)` constructor wrapping a JSON-array string to build an embedding value; libSQL-specific.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: With pgvector, bind the embedding as a string like '[1,2,3]'::vector or pass via the pg vector adapter; no vector() wrapper. Multi-row VALUES insert pattern is fine; convert `?`->$n and the per-row emb branch.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.snippet: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS nodes_fts_ai ... NODES_FTS_TRIGGER_DDL (AFTER INSERT trigger inserting into nodes_fts(rowid, body))
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: FTS5 external-content virtual table + a sync trigger keyed on rowid/ver; FTS5 is SQLite-specific.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: Use a tsvector column + GIN index (or a generated tsvector column), maintained by a trigger or GENERATED ALWAYS. The external-content+content_rowid model has no direct pg analog; redesign as a tsvector kept in sync. Design decision.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: FTS5 special 'rebuild' command to reindex an external-content table — pure FTS5 idiom.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: No equivalent; with tsvector the index is always live. Rebuild becomes a no-op or an UPDATE to repopulate the tsvector column. Drops out entirely under the pg model.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.snippet: INSERT INTO node_identity (id) VALUES ${part.map(()=>'(?)').join(',')} ... INSERT INTO node_versions (...) VALUES ${valuesSql}
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: Multi-row VALUES with positional `?` placeholders; chunkSize tuned to SQLite bound-arg limits.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: $n placeholders (or unnest($1::text[],...)) ; pg has a higher/different bound-param limit (65535) — chunkSize can change. VALUES multi-row insert is standard.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: SQLite ANALYZE refreshes sqlite_stat planner stats.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: Postgres ANALYZE [table] exists and is analogous; can keep, optionally target the table.

packages/core/src/bulk.ts.snippet: // One atomic `batch` (NOT `transaction()` — detaches connection from :memory: on this client build) ... await raw.batch(stmts, 'write')
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.whySqliteSpecific: libSQL Client.batch atomic batch; the comment notes a libSQL :memory: client quirk where transaction() detaches the connection.
packages/core/src/bulk.ts.postgresApproach: Use a real transaction (BEGIN/COMMIT) — the libSQL :memory: caveat does not apply to pg. Need a client abstraction since batch() is libSQL-only.

packages/core/src/control-plane.ts.snippet: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tenants (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL); ... role TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (role IN ('owner','editor','viewer')) ... created_at INTEGER
packages/core/src/control-plane.ts.whySqliteSpecific: SQLite type affinity: TEXT PRIMARY KEY for ULIDs, INTEGER for epoch-ms timestamps, scopes stored as TEXT (JSON). No native enum/timestamp/uuid types; CHECK simulates an enum.
packages/core/src/control-plane.ts.postgresApproach: Use real PG types: id TEXT or UUID PK, created_at BIGINT (epoch ms) or TIMESTAMPTZ, role as a CHECK or a CREATE TYPE role_enum AS ENUM(...), scopes as TEXT[] or jsonb. DDL is otherwise portable. Keep TEXT ids if ULIDs are kept.

packages/core/src/control-plane.ts.whySqliteSpecific: executeMultiple is a libSQL Client method that runs a multi-statement DDL script without ;-splitting; not a SQL standard. applyConnPragmas runs SQLite pragmas.
